nodes.label: Network-Latency Experiment Specification
nodes.rationale: Latency claims are interpretable only when metric, workload, baseline, topology, host and NIC configuration, timestamp boundary, and environment are recorded.

nodes.label: Coupled Fabric Control
nodes.rationale: Topology, congestion control, load balancing, job scheduling, and fabric scheduling interact and must be evaluated as one design problem.

nodes.label: Edge–Network Coordination Contract
nodes.rationale: Edge-centric and network-centric mechanisms require an explicit coordination contract.

nodes.label: Joint Tail-Latency and Goodput Evaluation
nodes.rationale: Excellent unloaded median latency can conceal queueing and scheduling failures under burst contention or near saturation.

nodes.label: Measure the Kernel Path First
nodes.rationale: DPDK is an architectural option only after the kernel path is measured and CPU reservation and operability costs are included.

nodes.label: Queue, Core, and NUMA Ownership
nodes.rationale: Queue concurrency assumptions, core placement, and memory-pool locality must be explicit.

nodes.label: Timestamp, Burst, and Recovery Boundaries
nodes.rationale: Benchmarks must define batch and burst behavior, timestamp boundaries, and failure/recovery handling.

nodes.label: Burst and Tail-Latency Testing
nodes.rationale: Queue-to-core changes vary by load point, so burst and tail behavior must replace universal queue-count rules.

nodes.label: Network Benchmark Configuration Record
nodes.rationale: Queue count, IRQ affinity, CPU placement, NUMA locality, interrupt moderation, socket options, and NIC settings belong in the record.

nodes.label: Network Timestamp Boundaries
nodes.rationale: Experiments must define whether time spans userspace, scheduler, driver, completion, or hardware boundaries.

nodes.label: Research Reading Critique Framework
nodes.rationale: Critiques assess problem framing, prior state, claimed contribution, evaluation soundness, bias, and durability.

nodes.label: Stanford CS244 — Advanced Topics in Networking
nodes.norm_label: stanford cs244 — advanced topics in networking

nodes.label: Failed Replication as Evidence
nodes.rationale: A documented failure can expose hidden assumptions and remains useful evidence.

nodes.label: Calibration Version and Regime Drift
nodes.rationale: Historical regime-dependent parameters require calibration versioning and drift checks before reuse.

nodes.label: Attainable Fill Constraint
nodes.rationale: Backtests must reject fills at signal prices that were not executable in the observed market.

nodes.label: Chronological Transaction-Cost-Aware Validation
nodes.rationale: Chronological holdouts and transaction-cost-aware objectives reduce temporal leakage and unrealistic performance.

nodes.label: Deterministic Full-Depth Replay Benchmark
nodes.rationale: Replay should be measured in events per second and latency distributions while remaining deterministic.

nodes.label: Agency-Execution Constraints
nodes.rationale: Specified target quantity and horizon require hard volume/time constraints, no-overfill assertions, and explicit terminal completion.

nodes.label: Causal Chronological Features
nodes.rationale: Execution evaluation must prevent future information from leaking into streaming features and train/test splits.

nodes.label: Deterministic Order-Book Replay
nodes.rationale: Adds, cancellations, partial fills, and executions must replay deterministically while hidden liquidity remains an explicit limitation.

nodes.label: Right-Censored Liquidity Estimation
nodes.rationale: Submitted size is not the same as observed available liquidity, so routing estimates must model censoring.

nodes.label: Latency, Throughput, Port, and Dependency Measurements
nodes.norm_label: latency, throughput, port, and dependency measurements

nodes.label: Independent Replication Process
nodes.rationale: Independent reimplementation of a precise published result tests whether the claimed result survives outside the original implementation and environment.

nodes.label: Deployment CPU Validation
nodes.rationale: Compiler, -march target, and observed performance must be validated on the actual deployment CPU.

nodes.label: Scheduling-Model Scope Limit
nodes.rationale: Default analysis omits or approximates fetch/decode, branch prediction, caches, memory hazards, and unsupported instructions.

nodes.label: Wall-Clock and Counter Corroboration
nodes.rationale: Scheduling-model predictions must be tested against distributions and hardware counters on the deployment CPU.

nodes.label: Application Workload and Counter Validation
nodes.rationale: Isolated instruction measurements do not predict caches, branches, OS interference, queues, or end-to-end latency.

nodes.label: Exact Instruction Form and CPU Matching
nodes.norm_label: exact instruction form and cpu matching
nodes.rationale: Instruction claims must match encoding, explicit and implicit operands, and the exact microarchitecture.

nodes.label: Separate Latency, Throughput, and Port Pressure
nodes.norm_label: separate latency, throughput, and port pressure
nodes.rationale: These measurements answer different bottleneck hypotheses and must not be treated as interchangeable.

nodes.label: ITCH Order-Lifecycle State Machine
nodes.rationale: Adds, executions, cancels, deletes, and replaces must be applied in sequence using order-reference links.

nodes.label: OUCH Order-State Machine
nodes.rationale: Every inbound action and outbound acceptance, fill, cancel, reject, restatement, or priority event must have an explicit transition.

nodes.label: Event-by-Event Trading-Ledger Reconciliation
nodes.rationale: Cash, inventory, P&L, orders, and fills must reconcile after every event to expose invisible execution errors.

nodes.label: Inventory, Fill, and P&L Reconciliation
nodes.rationale: Inventory must reconcile from fills, terminal inventory policy must be explicit, and fees and rebates belong in P&L.

nodes.label: Displayed-Book and Statistics Separation
nodes.rationale: Non-displayable trades, crosses, and broken trades do not all mutate displayed state in the same way.

nodes.label: Partial-Execution and Replace Invariants
nodes.rationale: Partial executions accumulate, zero quantity ends an order, replacement retires the old reference, and inherited fields must be retained.

nodes.label: Protocol-Revision-Pinned Feed Fixtures
nodes.rationale: Exact lengths, types, headers, timestamps, and lifecycle edge cases must be tied to the captured protocol revision.

nodes.label: Monotonic User-Reference Invariant
nodes.rationale: User references are day-unique and increasing and must be checked across requests and recovery.

nodes.label: Replace, Partial-Cancel, and Priority Semantics
nodes.rationale: Liability and priority changes cannot be collapsed into a generic update.

nodes.label: Retransmission and Mirrored-Session Recovery
nodes.rationale: Benign duplicates, sequential connection processing, and fault-redundant hosts require explicit recovery tests.

nodes.label: Data-Movement Cost Model
nodes.rationale: Movement from memory to registers dominates many numerical kernels and motivates blocking, packing, and register reuse.

nodes.label: Memory-Hierarchy Traffic Model
nodes.rationale: Transformations should be explained by the memory-hierarchy level whose traffic they change.

nodes.label: Numerical-Correctness Acceptance Gates
nodes.rationale: Runtime improvements are acceptable only when residuals, errors, convergence, feasibility, and explicit tolerances remain valid.

nodes.label: Structure-Aware Optimization
nodes.rationale: Symmetry, sparsity, or low rank may be exploited only when guaranteed by the model.

nodes.label: Performance Curves Across Realistic Sizes
nodes.rationale: Performance across representative sizes is more reliable than optimizing one convenient matrix.

nodes.label: Reference Implementation and Correctness Oracle
nodes.rationale: A reference implementation is preserved so every optimized variant can be checked for correctness.

nodes.norm_label: eth zurich — how to write fast numerical code

nodes.label: Staged Kernel Transformations
nodes.rationale: Keeping explicit variants makes each optimization's contribution inspectable.

nodes.label: Runtime Feature Selection
nodes.rationale: Heterogeneous deployments need runtime selection or separately built variants plus a tested fallback path.

nodes.label: Runtime Dispatch for Heterogeneous CPUs
nodes.rationale: Target-specific flags or binaries must be isolated and selected safely across heterogeneous deployments.

nodes.label: Generation-Specific Optimization
nodes.rationale: Advice must be selected for the exact processor generation because cache, branch, load/store, and SIMD behavior varies.

nodes.label: Processor-Family-Specific Optimization
nodes.rationale: Processor behavior and errata vary, so guidance must be pinned to family or stepping and manual revision.

nodes.label: Generated Assembly Inspection
nodes.rationale: Portable SIMD abstractions remain hypotheses until emitted code and representative benchmarks are checked on the server.

nodes.label: Scalar Oracle and Tail Correctness
nodes.rationale: Target-specific SIMD must preserve scalar results and handle alignment and non-vector-length tails correctly.

nodes.label: Emitted Instruction Inspection
nodes.rationale: Vendor guidance explains a candidate transformation, but emitted instructions and target-machine measurements determine whether it helps.

nodes.label: Version- and Target-Pinned Analysis
nodes.rationale: Compiler, flags, target triple, -mcpu, region, iterations, and LLVM version define the prediction.
